newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus opposition to Lukashenko down but not out.
newsitem.headline: Belarus opposition to Lukashenko down but not out.

text.p: Opponents of hardline President Alexander Lukashenko, beaten for now in their fight to stop him seizing more authority, claimed the moral high ground on Tuesday but conceded they were all but powerless.
As pro-Lukashenko deputies formed a breakaway parliament near his residence, communists, agrarians, liberals and democrats met in the old chamber to discuss their next move.
The opposition said they would wait for Lukashenko's deputies, meeting elsewhere, to return as they lacked the two-thirds majority the constitution says they need to form a new parliament.

"We have the strongest force there is -- moral right is on our side," speaker Semyon Sharetsky told a grim chamber as it became clear Lukashenko had the support of a majority of deputies, enough for a quorum.
Out of 199 members of the old parliament, 112 have gone over to the president's side. The opposition said they had been bought by promises of new cars and apartments.
"Let's stay honest to the end. Let's not go begging on our knees for crumbs at the president's table," one deputy, Ivan Shulakovsky, told 66 deputies at an afternoon session.
A pro-Lukashenko deputy, Yuri Kulikovsky, told Reuters they would form a new "House of Representatives" on Tuesday and move back to the old building this week.

"Let him (Lukashenko) do what he wants. You should never pay attention to people who fly into rages and completely disregard the law," Sharetsky told Reuters. "We follow the power of laws. But there, they follow the law of power," he added.
Lukashenko won an overwhelming mandate to form a new legislature in a referendum on Sunday after an extremely one-sided campaign which critics said was fraudulent.
Lukashenko had ignored the old constitution, the constitutional court and parliamentary votes to press ahead with the referendum and made it legally binding by decree.
"What referendum? It was a rape of the people," Sharetsky retorted when asked for his evaluation of the vote.
Sharetsky was encouraged by a statement from the U.S. State Department describing the vote in Belarus as illegitimate, and by a visit from a European Parliament delegation.
But he said he was saddened by the impression the president's electoral victory would give other countries of his nation of 10 million between Russia and Poland.
"They look at us as if to say: 'Are they crazy?' We are a hard-working, peace-loving people, conscientious people...which has subjected itself to violence and deceit," he said.

Sharetsky was hopeful of some help from neighbouring Russia, Minsk's main ally, though the Kremlin has signalled it was unlikely to interfere with Lukashenko's plans providing he managed to resolve the situation without violence.

Gennady Karpenko, a leading communist deputy opposed to Lukashenko, was also hopeful of help from Western Europe. The European Union issued a statement on Tuesday expressing concern about events in Belarus.
"I am sure we will be supported by the European Community," he told Reuters.

But he was clearly saddened by the results of the referendum, in which only about one third of the electorate voted to ban off-budget funds and for direct elections of regional officials who are appointed by Lukashenko.
"We have reduced our nation to the point where it does not want to know how the budget is spent, or to elect officials. It wants nearly nothing. That's what saddens me most," he said.
